title: Practitioner Exam
description: 35 questions covering all five modules, drawn from a pool of 44. Pass mark is 80%. This is an open-book exam — take your time, browse any module to refresh your memory, or ask the AI assistant for help. Your answers are saved as you go, so leaving the page to look something up is fine. Explanations show after submission so you can learn from any answers you missed.

questions.scenario: A finance analyst needs to slice revenue by product, region, and quarter, with quick drill-down to find the story behind the numbers.
questions.prompt: Which Pentaho Business Analytics tool is the right starting point?
options: Dashboard Designer
Analyzer (PAZ)
Interactive Reports (PIR)
Pentaho Data Integration
questions.explanation: Analyzer's OLAP-backed pivot is built for slice-and-dice exploration and drill-down. Interactive Reports targets tabular reports; Dashboard Designer composes pre-built views; PDI is ETL.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Overview — Choosing the right tool

questions.scenario: An executive wants a one-page view combining five charts and a KPI panel, all driven by a single date filter.
questions.prompt: Which tool fits this requirement best?
options: Dashboard Designer (PDD)
Analyzer
Interactive Reports
Schema Workbench
questions.explanation: Dashboard Designer composes multiple visualisations onto one canvas and wires shared prompts. Analyzer explores one cube; Interactive Reports builds tabular reports; Schema Workbench models OLAP cubes.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Overview — Choosing the right tool

questions.scenario: A regional manager just needs a tabular grouped report by Territory and Sales Rep with subtotals — no charts, no exploration.
questions.prompt: Which tool is the best fit?
options: Analyzer
Interactive Reports
Dashboard Designer
Pentaho Server admin console
questions.explanation: Grouped tabular reports against a curated metadata model are the Interactive Reports sweet spot. Analyzer would over-tool the problem; a dashboard is heavier than needed.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Overview — Choosing the right tool

questions.prompt: Defining the data once as a reusable model or data source and referencing it from many reports delivers what benefit?
options: It saves disk space
Centralised governance — connection or model changes propagate to every consumer, and security can be enforced once at the model layer
Reports run faster automatically
It allows offline use
questions.explanation: One model and many consumers is the BI governance pattern. Change the connection or row-level security once at the model, and every report inherits it. Without it, each report is its own silo.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Overview — Data governance

questions.scenario: A team must email the EMEA Quantity report to regional leads on the first of every month without anyone running it by hand.
questions.prompt: When is scheduling a report most useful?
options: When the data never changes
When an audience needs a consistent cadence of the same parameterised report and you want to avoid each consumer running it manually
When the report has prompts
When the report cannot be opened in PUC
questions.explanation: Scheduling delivers the same view on a cadence to a known audience. Pair it with parameterised reports so one definition serves many recipient lists.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: User Console — Schedules

questions.prompt: Why is the data model (cubes, metadata) usually kept under change control in a Pentaho BI deployment?
options: The model is decorative
Every report, dashboard, and Analyzer view depends on it, so a schema change ripples to every consumer — the model is treated like production software with versioning and review
Models are auto-generated from queries
Schemas are immutable after first publish
questions.explanation: Models are foundational. A breaking change to a hierarchy or measure cascades to every consumer, so change control protects the consumer surface.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Overview — Data governance

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between self-service BI and managed reporting?
options: Self-service uses spreadsheets; managed uses databases
Self-service lets curated end users author their own ad-hoc views against governed models, while managed reporting delivers IT-built reports to consumers who read but don't author
Managed reporting always runs in the cloud
Self-service is faster than managed reporting
questions.explanation: Both flow from the same governed models, but self-service hands authoring to the user while managed reporting keeps authoring with IT and delivers finished reports.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Overview — Self-service vs managed reporting

questions.scenario: EMEA managers should see only EMEA rows in every report they open, while NA managers see only NA rows — from the same report definitions.
questions.prompt: What does row-level security mean in this BI deployment?
options: Each row is encrypted at rest
Users see different subsets of the same query results based on their identity or role, enforced at the model layer rather than re-implemented in every report
Reports run row by row instead of in batch
Rows are sorted by user role
questions.explanation: Row-level security lives at the model so every consumer of every report inherits it. Without that pattern, security must be re-implemented in each report and is easy to bypass.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Overview — Data governance

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of the Pentaho User Console (PUC) for a business user?
options: A command-line tool for editing transformations
A browser-based hub for browsing data sources, opening reports and dashboards, and scheduling jobs
A standalone Windows application for database administration
A REST API client
questions.explanation: PUC is the web-based front door of the Pentaho Server. Business users open and create reports, browse data sources, and manage schedules from the browser.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: User Console — Pentaho User Console

questions.prompt: Why is browser-based delivery, rather than a desktop client install, the standard model for end users?
options: Browsers are faster than native applications
Zero-install rollout, centralised content and permissions, easier upgrades, and consistent access across devices
Native apps cannot render charts
It is required by HTTPS
questions.explanation: The browser model decouples the user from the install. IT updates the server once and every user benefits — no client install, no version drift, no per-laptop access control.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: User Console — Pentaho User Console

questions.prompt: What is the typical relationship between data sources and reports in PUC?
options: Reports embed copies of the underlying data
Data sources expose business-friendly models or queries, and reports read from them to present the results visually
Reports always pull live data from CSV files only
Data sources are uploaded inside each report file
questions.explanation: Data sources are reusable abstractions (JDBC, OLAP/Analysis, metadata). Reports reference them, so administrators can change the underlying connection without rewriting every report.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: User Console — Data sources

questions.prompt: The Home, Browse Files, and Schedules perspectives in PUC reflect which design pattern?
options: Random feature placement
Task-oriented navigation — landing pages for what business users actually do (open content, find content, manage delivery) rather than mirroring the back-end folder structure
A database-administrator workflow
A developer / IDE workflow
questions.explanation: PUC is organised by user task, not by repository layout. That keeps non-technical users productive without learning the server's internal folder hierarchy.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: User Console — Perspectives

questions.prompt: Permissions in PUC are typically enforced where?
options: In the browser, after the report renders
On the server, before content is returned, based on the user's role and the content's ACLs / model-level security
On the local file system of each user's laptop
In the CSS layer
questions.explanation: Authorisation lives server-side so it can't be bypassed by a different client. Content ACLs and the model's security together decide what each user sees.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: User Console — Users & Roles

questions.scenario: An analyst has just authored a report and must decide whether to save it to a shared Public folder or to their personal Home folder.
questions.prompt: How do these two save locations differ in PUC?
options: Folder location is cosmetic only
Shared (Public) folders make content discoverable and runnable by other users subject to permissions, while Home folders are personal scratch space
Shared folders compress the file
Home folders are encrypted
questions.explanation: Save location is a publishing decision. Personal versus team scope is set by folder; that, plus permissions, controls who can find and use the content.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: User Console — Browse Files

questions.prompt: What problem does Interactive Reports solve compared with a fully designer-built report?
options: It produces faster SQL than Report Designer
It lets non-technical users build ad-hoc tabular and grouped reports against a curated metadata model — no SQL, no IT round-trip
It can render 3D charts
It is the only tool that can export PDFs
questions.explanation: Interactive Reports targets the business user who needs a quick tabular answer. The metadata model hides joins and SQL, so the user just picks fields, filters, and groupings.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Overview

questions.scenario: An analyst building a Sales Territory report wants to turn a flat list of orders into a scannable layout with one section per territory.
questions.prompt: What does grouping the report by Territory and adding a subtotal achieve?
options: It doubles the number of rows in the source table
It collapses the data into one section per group, with aggregated measures and a running total — far more scannable than raw rows
It hides the column header
It makes the report run slower on purpose
questions.explanation: Grouping plus subtotals is the standard pattern for turning a flat list into a business-ready report. Each group becomes a section with its own measures.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Sales Territory

questions.prompt: What does a prompt (parameter) in an Interactive Report let the consumer do?
options: Edit the SQL inline
Pick a value at run time (e.g. Year = 2024, Region = EMEA) so one report definition can serve many scenarios
Switch the report into a chart automatically
Bypass row-level security
questions.explanation: Prompts parameterise the report. One definition plus run-time values yields many concrete results, cutting maintenance and letting self-service users explore.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Prompts

questions.prompt: Why does page setup (orientation, headers/footers, page size) matter when authoring an Interactive Report?
options: It changes the underlying data
Reports are commonly exported or printed, and page setup controls how the layout breaks across pages so totals and group headers aren't orphaned
It is required to save the report at all
It affects how fast the report runs
questions.explanation: Output formatting matters because reports often leave the browser as emailed PDFs or printed packs. Good page setup keeps the layout coherent across page breaks.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Page setup

questions.scenario: NA and EMEA both need essentially the same orders report, differing only by region and totals.
questions.prompt: What is usually the right authoring approach?
options: Build two separate reports and maintain both
Build one parameterised report driven by a Region prompt, optionally with two saved schedules feeding different recipient lists
Combine NA and EMEA into one global region
Copy-paste the SQL into Excel
questions.explanation: One parameterised template plus saved schedules per audience is the standard pattern — lower maintenance, easier to evolve, and every region gets the same shape.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Orders NA and EMEA

questions.prompt: What complexity does the metadata model behind Interactive Reports hide from the business user?
options: Colour choices
Joins, key columns, technical table names, and relationships — replaced by business-friendly fields such as Customers and Orders
Page sizing
Schedule timing
questions.explanation: The metadata model translates the physical schema into a business vocabulary. The user picks Sales Amount and Territory instead of navigating a join graph between fact and dimension tables.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Metadata model

questions.scenario: A report needs a Margin column, but Margin isn't defined in the metadata — only Revenue and Cost are.
questions.prompt: When is a computed field / formula column the right answer?
options: When you want a new report file
When a measure isn't pre-defined in the metadata but can be derived from existing fields, e.g. Margin = Revenue − Cost
When you need a new database
When the report needs a different page layout
questions.explanation: Computed fields keep authoring agile — the user derives the field they need without going back to the metadata team to add it permanently.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Computed fields

questions.prompt: In what order are filtering, sorting, and grouping applied in an Interactive Report?
options: At random points in the rendering
Filters narrow the rows first, then sorting orders the remaining set, then subtotals and group breaks layer onto the sorted output
Only after export
Only in the client browser
questions.explanation: Filter, then sort, then group is the consistent order. Filtering first reduces work, sorting establishes iteration order, and grouping then breaks the stream into sections.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Filtering & sorting

questions.prompt: Which output formats can an Interactive Report be exported to?
options: HTML
PDF
CSV
Excel
questions.explanation: Interactive Reports can be output as HTML, PDF, CSV, or Excel files — CSV/Excel for downstream tooling, PDF/HTML for human consumption. The format follows the audience.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Output formats

questions.scenario: A Ships and Trains report needs to combine two related datasets into one coherent view.
questions.prompt: What is the cleanest authoring pattern?
options: Build separate reports and hope users open both
Pre-join the data in the metadata model and report against one logical view, or use shared prompts so both datasets respond to the same context
Use a different tool entirely
Manually concatenate exports
questions.explanation: Reporting against pre-joined metadata keeps the report simple. Failing that, shared prompts keep parallel datasets in sync from the user's point of view.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Interactive Reports — Ships and Trains

questions.prompt: Because Analyzer is backed by a Mondrian OLAP model, which interactions can a user perform directly on the data?
options: Drill, slice, dice, and pivot the cube
Filter data and add calculated fields
Rewrite the report's SQL by hand at run time
Edit the rows in the underlying fact table
questions.explanation: The Mondrian model lets users drill, slice, dice, pivot, filter, chart data, and create calculated fields — without knowing how the database is structured. Analyzer is for analysis, not for editing source rows or hand-writing SQL.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — OLAP & Mondrian

questions.scenario: An analyst viewing sales by Year clicks Year to expand it into Quarters while keeping every other part of the view unchanged.
questions.prompt: What is this operation called?
options: Reducing the row count by random sampling
Drill-down — moving from a higher level of a hierarchy (Year) to the level below it (Quarter) while keeping the rest of the context constant
Switching from a chart to a table
Changing the database connection
questions.explanation: Drill-down walks down a hierarchy one level. The Year-level aggregate becomes Quarter-level while the rest of the slice (region, product, etc.) stays put.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — Drill-down

questions.scenario: A sales manager wants underperforming cells to jump out, turning a dense grid into an at-a-glance status display.
questions.prompt: Why is conditional formatting (stop-lighting) on a measure useful here?
options: It changes the actual data values
Visual cues let consumers spot exceptions in seconds without reading every number
It is required before the report can be saved
It speeds up query execution
questions.explanation: Conditional stop-lighting shifts cognitive load from the reader to the layout. Red / amber / green cells direct attention to the rows that need action.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — Conditional formatting

questions.prompt: A tree map visualisation is best for what kind of question?
options: Comparing a time series across many years
Showing the relative size of nested categories — e.g. quantity sold per territory within EMEA — using area to encode magnitude
Displaying a binary yes/no status
Plotting geographic coordinates
questions.explanation: Tree maps encode hierarchical part-of-whole relationships with area, making 'who is biggest within this group' visible at a glance.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — Visualisations

questions.prompt: Filtering by Year while keeping Territory broken out is an example of which OLAP concept?
options: Slicing — restricting one dimension to a value or set while leaving other dimensions free to vary
Pivoting — swapping rows and columns
Dicing — restricting multiple dimensions simultaneously
Joining — combining two fact tables
questions.explanation: Slicing pins one dimension (Year = 2024) and lets the rest vary. Dicing pins several; pivoting reorganises rows and columns. All are interactive moves Analyzer supports.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — Slice, dice, pivot

questions.prompt: Why is hierarchy-aware modelling (Country → Region → City) more useful in Analyzer than a flat list of geographies?
options: It makes the schema file smaller
Hierarchies let the user drill seamlessly without rebuilding the query, and roll-ups aggregate measures automatically at each level
Hierarchies are required for charts to render
It controls user permissions
questions.explanation: Hierarchies are the navigation skeleton. Drill-up and drill-down are free, and aggregations at each level happen automatically.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — Hierarchies

questions.scenario: Several Analyzer views, a dashboard, and an Interactive Report all need Margin % = Revenue / Cost − 1, computed identically everywhere.
questions.prompt: Where is the best place to define that calculated measure?
options: In every report individually
In the schema (cube), so every Analyzer view, dashboard, and dependent report inherits the same definition
In the browser
In the HTTP layer
questions.explanation: Shared calculations belong with the model. Every consumer gets the same definition and changes propagate; per-report definitions cause subtle drift.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — Calculated measures

questions.prompt: Why does drill-through (clicking a cell to see the underlying detail rows) complement OLAP?
options: It is required for accessibility
OLAP excels at aggregates, and drill-through reveals the detail records that produced an aggregate — the 'why' behind the number
It changes the database connection
It is faster than drill-down
questions.explanation: Aggregates answer 'how much'; detail rows answer 'which records'. Drill-through bridges the two without forcing the user into a different tool.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — Drill-through

questions.prompt: Moving Year from rows to columns to re-shape an Analyzer report is called:
options: Drill-down
Pivoting — reorganising the dimensions to reveal patterns the original orientation hid
Slicing
Joining
questions.explanation: Pivoting reorganises how dimensions lay out in the grid. It often surfaces patterns the original orientation hid, without changing the data or filters.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — Slice, dice, pivot

questions.prompt: What is the job of the Mondrian (Analysis Schema) layer?
options: Rendering the chart
Translating multidimensional queries (MDX) into efficient SQL against the relational warehouse and aggregating the results into cube form
Scheduling reports
Storing the cube in a binary file
questions.explanation: Mondrian is the OLAP engine. It defines dimensions, hierarchies, and measures over a relational source and converts user-issued MDX into SQL on demand.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Analyzer Reports — OLAP & Mondrian

questions.prompt: Which content types can be placed in a Dashboard Designer panel?
options: Charts created with Chart Designer
Data Tables and Interactive Reporting / Analyzer content
URLs (an external web page in a panel)
Raw Spoon transformation canvases
questions.explanation: A dashboard composes content from Interactive Reporting and Analyzer plus Charts (Chart Designer), Data Tables, and URLs into one at-a-glance view. It does not embed the PDI transformation canvas itself.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Overview

questions.scenario: A dashboard has five panels, and a single Year picker should drive all of them so the consumer never compares mismatched filters.
questions.prompt: What benefit do shared dashboard prompts deliver?
options: They reduce the file size of the dashboard
Consistency — every panel responds to the same context, so the consumer never compares visualisations across mismatched filters
They are required for the dashboard to save
They prevent users from drilling down
questions.explanation: When one prompt drives every panel, the dashboard is always internally consistent. Without shared prompts, comparing panels becomes a trap because they may be filtered differently.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Filters & content linking

questions.scenario: A vendor-sales dashboard loads slowly because each panel issues its own overlapping query at render time.
questions.prompt: What is usually the most effective design improvement?
options: Switch to a different colour palette
Reduce the number of independent queries — pre-aggregate at the data layer, share queries across panels, or cache results
Re-export the dashboard as PDF
Increase the browser zoom level
questions.explanation: Dashboard latency is usually query-bound. Pre-aggregating, caching, or sharing one query across visualisations cuts database round trips dramatically.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Vendor Sales

questions.scenario: An inventory dashboard pairs a total inventory value KPI with per-SKU detail panels underneath.
questions.prompt: What is the rationale for this layout?
options: To consume more screen space
Top-down information design — the headline tells the consumer whether to investigate, and the detail panels answer the follow-up without leaving the page
Dashboards must always have at least four panels
To run more queries
questions.explanation: The standard pattern is headline first, supporting detail underneath. Consumers see the summary, decide whether to drill, and stay on one page if they do.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Inventory

questions.scenario: A product-performance dashboard combines a ranked list of products with a trend chart.
questions.prompt: What is the design rationale for pairing these two visualisations?
options: Variety for variety's sake
The list answers 'which products' and the trend answers 'is performance improving or declining', so together they support diagnosis and action
Two visualisations are required by the framework
Trend charts can only sit next to ranked lists
questions.explanation: Distinct visualisations answer distinct questions. Lists order, trends show direction. Pairing them makes the dashboard usable for both 'who' and 'where are they going'.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Product Performance

questions.prompt: Why are drill-through links (clicking a chart bar to open a detailed report) useful on a dashboard?
options: They double the number of dashboards
They let consumers stay on the summary by default and jump to detail only when needed, keeping the dashboard fast and uncluttered
They are required for accessibility
They cache the underlying data
questions.explanation: Drill-through is progressive disclosure. The dashboard stays light and detail is available on demand, so consumers don't pay for rendering detail they didn't ask for.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Drill-through

questions.scenario: One vendor-sales dashboard must serve both NA and EMEA business units, each seeing only its own data.
questions.prompt: What is the typical pattern?
options: Build a separate dashboard per unit
Build one dashboard, parameterise it with a region prompt, and let permissions / row-level security narrow the data each user sees
Combine all units into one big total
Build a third dashboard summarising the others
questions.explanation: One parameterised dashboard plus row-level security scales naturally. Each consumer sees a personalised view from the same definition — far less to maintain than a dashboard per unit.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Vendor Sales

questions.prompt: What should primarily drive the choice of chart type for a dashboard panel?
options: The author's aesthetic preference
The question the consumer needs to answer — counts, trends, proportions, and relationships each call for a different chart family
Whichever chart loads fastest
Whatever was used in the last dashboard
questions.explanation: Chart type is a function of the question: bars for comparison, lines for trend, treemaps for hierarchical proportion, scatter for correlation. Aesthetics come after function.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Chart selection

questions.prompt: When two panels in a dashboard need the same underlying query, what is the cleanest pattern?
options: Issue the query twice for safety
Define the query once and let both panels read the same result — fewer database round trips and guaranteed consistency
Hard-code the panel data
Run each panel sequentially
questions.explanation: A shared query is both the optimisation lever and the consistency lever. Define once, render twice. Independent queries can drift slightly and double the database load.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Queries

questions.prompt: When a dashboard layout breaks at small screen sizes, what is usually the right response?
options: Force users to use larger monitors
Design with responsive proportions and stacking from the start, prioritising headline panels and letting detail wrap or collapse on smaller widths
Lock the layout to a single resolution
Remove all charts on mobile
questions.explanation: Design for variability. Headline panels first, supporting panels collapse or wrap. The dashboard should degrade gracefully across the screens consumers actually use.
questions.source: Pentaho Analyst - Practitioner: Dashboard Designer — Layout templates
